extracted.intended_audience: ethnologists / field anthropologists / travellers collecting folklore in West Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for collectors and observers working among West African peoples: how to collect, record, interpret, and classify stories, charms, spirits, and ritual behaviour while avoiding bias and over-generalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep original material carefully noted at time of occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember, you must always have your original material--carefully noted down at the time of occurrence--with you, so that you may say in answer to his Why? Because of this, and this, and this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tag and preserve provenance (locality, tribe, conditions) for each story or datum; do not submit unattributed piles of tales to an ethnologist — context is essential to resolve apparent contradictions and pointlessness. Examples: ticket stories with the culture/tribe and local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ticket tales with cultural/contextual information
rubrics_metrics.description: If you were to bring home a heap of stories ... without ticketing them with the culture of the tribe they belonged to, the conditions it lives under, and so forth, you would stun him with the seeming inter-contradiction of some, and utter pointlessness of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always record tribe, locality, social conditions, and circumstances of collection; contextual metadata is required to make sense of narratives and avoid misleading synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature over-generalisation when a single 'key' explains some facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have found the easy key that opens the reason underlying a series of facts ... do not, when you have found this key, drop your collecting work, and go home with a shriek of 'I know all about Fetish,' because you don't, for the key to the above facts will not open the reason why ... This set requires another key entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat tentative explanatory keys as partial; keep collecting to find additional keys for other clusters of phenomena. Example: one explanation for greetings and avoidance behaviours will not explain burial or nail-paring customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect your mind from bias; recognise untrustworthiness of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Your own mind requires protection ... The best protection lies in recognising the untrustworthiness of human evidence regarding the unseen, and also the seen, when it is viewed by a person who has in his mind an explanation of the phenomenon before it occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selecting only facts that fit preconceived notions; emulate the marine engineer metaphor—carefully watch, maintain, and test observations rather than forcing them to fit theory. Example anti-pattern: cherry-picking anecdotes that confirm a favored explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use failures as informative as successes
rubrics_metrics.description: A careful study of the things a man, black or white, fails to do, whether for good or evil, usually gives you a truer knowledge of the man than the things he succeeds in doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record both what people do and what they notably do not or cannot do (mechanical arts, craft production, writing) — absences can reveal cognitive or cultural emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify spirits by function (use functional taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying them is therefore a difficult work, but Doctor Nassau thinks this may be done fairly completely into: 1. Human disembodied spirits--Manu. 2. Vague beings, well described by our word ghosts: Abambo. 3. Beings something like dryads ... Ombwiri. 4. Beings who are the agents in causing sickness ... Mionde. 5. Household spirits ... oginga. 6. Those that enter into any animal body ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a functional classification (origin, habitation, role, e.g., household guardians, disease-causers, territorial spirits, animal-possession). Note overlap: different classes may perform identical functions; classify primarily by function rather than trying to 'weigh and measure' spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note variability and limits of individual spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are characteristics that all the authorities seem agreed on, and one is that individual spirits in the same class vary in power: some are strong of their sort, some weak. They are all to a certain extent limited in the nature of their power; there is no one spirit that can do all things; their efficiency only runs in certain lines of action ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing reports of spirit action, account for gradations of potency and domain-specific abilities rather than assuming uniform agency; this helps explain inconsistent outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charms: method, materials, and intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of making these charms ... the spirit is induced to localise itself in some object ... things most frequently used are antelopes' horns, the large snail-shells, and large nutshells ... pineapple fibre sausage shape ... outside coloured red to flatter and please him ... The substance put inside charms is all manner of nastiness ... nature of the substance depends on the spirit it is intended to be attractive to ... charms made to influence a person ... must have in them some portion of the person to be dealt with--his hair, blood, nail-parings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting or analysing charms, record construction materials, colour symbolism (red ~ blood), contents, and whether personal items of the target are included; interpret items functionally (attraction, association, symbolic efficacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess charms' social ecology and failure modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing you wish of them may, and frequently does, happen ... other times it does not. In Africa this is held to arise from the bad character of the spirits; their gross ingratitude and fickleness. ... the spirit has been lured away ... or that he finds the spirit is dead; it has been killed by a more powerful spirit of its class, which is in the pay of some enemy of yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate interpersonal competition, theft of spirits, and economic transactions (buying more powerful charms) as explanatory variables for charm success/failure. Record follow-up claims about why charms ceased to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link sacrifice value to the requested favour
rubrics_metrics.description: The sacrifice is the usual killing of something valuable as an offering to the spirits. The value of the offering in these S.W. Coast regions has certainly a regular relationship to the value of the favour required of the spirits. Some favours are worth a dish of plantains, some a fowl, some a goat and some a human being, though human sacrifice is very rare ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting ritual economics, note the correspondence between offering cost/value and desired outcome; also record beliefs about 'intention ennobles the gift' and cases where symbolic offerings are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat prohibitions (Orunda/Ibet) as sacred dedications rather than arbitrary taboos
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain rites are performed for children ... a prohibition is laid upon the child as regards the eating of some particular article of food ... the prohibited article is a sacrifice ordained for the child by its parents and the magic doctor as a gift to the governing spirit of its life. The thing prohibited becom(es) removed from the child's common use, and is made sacred to the spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record prohibitions along with their ritual framing and purported function (gift to governing spirit), and avoid assuming the taboo is simply superstition; seek local explanations, ceremony, and sanctions for breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ascribe single causes; allow multiple explanations for same practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Great care is requisite in these matters, because a man may do or abstain from doing one and the same thing for divers reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or interpreting behaviour, permit multiple causal attributions (personal Orunda, social status, purity rules, pragmatic reasons) and triangulate with informant testimony, ritual context, and comparative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for native explanatory frameworks about death (witchcraft, bush-soul, reincarnation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their lives are dominated by a profound belief in witchcraft ... rule is that death is regarded as a direct consequence of the witchcraft of some malevolent human being ... exceptions: bush-soul (every man has four souls ... bush-soul may cause sickness) ... another way ... part of this disease may get reincarnated with him and then he will ultimately die of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying mortality and causation beliefs, document local ontologies (witchcraft agency, bush-soul, reincarnation, disease inheritance) and how these co-exist or compete in explanations of illness and death.
